explanations.answer: Because the LORD their God is holy
explanations.explanation: That's the reason right there in the verse: “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.” (Leviticus 19:2) God doesn't point to a rule or a crowd. He points to who He is. And He says it to the whole congregation of Israel, so nobody gets to sit this one out.

explanations.answer: Because the nations are watching them
explanations.explanation: The verse never mentions anybody watching, friend. God gives one reason, and it's about Himself: “…because I, the LORD your God, am holy.” (Leviticus 19:2) I'll admit an audience sounds like a good reason. It's just not the one God gave.

explanations.answer: Because they are about to enter the land
explanations.explanation: The land does come up later in this chapter, but not as the reason for holiness. Here God says, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.” (Leviticus 19:2) The reason He gives is who He is. That's the one to hold onto.

That's it. God says each person “…must respect his mother and father…” (Leviticus 19:3) Both parents get named, so neither one gets skipped. That's a good place to start holy living, right at the kitchen table.

A teacher is a fine person to respect, but that's not who God names here. The verse says, “Each of you must respect his mother and father…” (Leviticus 19:3) He starts with the family. Close to home, like I said.

Master is a word you'd expect in a lot of places, but not in this verse. God says, “Each of you must respect his mother and father…” (Leviticus 19:3) Those are the two He names. Right alongside that, He says, “…you must keep My Sabbaths.”

True, friend. God says, “Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods.” (Leviticus 19:4) That's two things: don't turn to idols, and don't make molten gods. Then He signs it the way He signed the last command: “I am the LORD your God.”

It's actually true. The verse says, “Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods.” (Leviticus 19:4) God says it plainly, and no exceptions are listed. And He closes the command with “I am the LORD your God.”

Right. “…what remains on the third day must be burned up.” (Leviticus 19:6) The offering gets two days to be eaten, the day you sacrifice it or the next. After that, there's no day three for the leftovers. The next verse says if any of it is eaten on the third day, it “…is tainted and will not be accepted.” (Leviticus 19:7)
The verse doesn't send the leftovers to anyone. It says what remains on the third day “…must be burned up.” (Leviticus 19:6) So the third day is the end of the line for that offering. No handoff.

Salted and stored, friend? That's a good move for a pantry, but not for this offering. God says what remains on the third day “…must be burned up.” (Leviticus 19:6) I've left plenty of things in the back of a drawer for years, but this offering doesn't get that treatment. Day three, it goes in the fire.

It's the other way around. God says, “If any of it is eaten on the third day, it is tainted and will not be accepted.” (Leviticus 19:7) The day matters here. Two days is the window, and the third day is closed.

False is right. The verse says, “If any of it is eaten on the third day, it is tainted and will not be accepted.” (Leviticus 19:7) Tainted and not accepted, that's how plainly God puts it. So the third-day rule is no small thing.

You got it. “Leave them for the poor and the foreigner.” (Leviticus 19:10) The same goes for the edges of the field and the gleanings from verse 9. So God has the harvest leave something on the table for people who need it. And He signs it, “I am the LORD your God.”

Good guess, friend. Priests and Levites are a fair thing to think of. But for the harvest, God points somewhere else. He says to leave the fallen grapes “…for the poor and the foreigner.” (Leviticus 19:10) So those grapes stay on the ground for them. Think of it as a batch of cookies where you leave a few on the cooling rack on purpose.

Hired hands do show up in this chapter, but later, and it's about their pay. For the grapes, God says, “Leave them for the poor and the foreigner.” (Leviticus 19:10) Those are the two He names. I'd stick with His list.

Profane is the word. “You must not swear falsely by My name and so profane the name of your God.” (Leviticus 19:12) Swearing falsely drags God's own name into a lie. And God closes it with “I am the LORD…”

Protect sounds nice, but it's the opposite of what's said. The verse reads, “You must not swear falsely by My name and so profane the name of your God.” (Leviticus 19:12) A false oath doesn't guard His name. It profanes it.

A false oath is the farthest thing from honor, friend. The verse says it would “…profane the name of your God.” (Leviticus 19:12) Swearing by His name is serious, so it has to be true. And He seals it with “I am the LORD…”

Yes. “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand.” (Leviticus 19:13) The pay is due before morning comes. That's a short deadline, friend. Payday doesn't get to hit the snooze button.

explanations.answer: By the end of the week
explanations.explanation: That's a lot longer than God allows. The verse says, “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand.” (Leviticus 19:13) So the pay is due before morning, not at the end of the week. That's a short deadline, friend.

Harvest does come up in this chapter, but not as a payday. God says, “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand.” (Leviticus 19:13) Wages don't wait on the harvest. They don't even wait on the sunrise.

The verse has no loophole like that. God says, “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God.” (Leviticus 19:14) Nothing in it depends on whether anyone can tell who did it. The command ends with “I am the LORD…”

False is right. “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God.” (Leviticus 19:14) There's no "unless they can't tell" clause tucked in there. The command stands as written, and it ends with “I am the LORD…”

It's the reverse. God says, “You must not pervert justice; you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly.” (Leviticus 19:15) A little extra favor for the poor is exactly the partiality He rules out. Fair means fair, and it goes both ways, poor and rich.

False is right. The verse says, “you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly.” (Leviticus 19:15) The scale doesn't tip toward either side. A neighbor is a neighbor, and each one gets a fair hearing.

True. “You must not go about spreading slander among your people.” (Leviticus 19:16) The command is about going around with it among your own people. The same verse adds, “You must not endanger the life of your neighbor.” Then it closes with “I am the LORD…”

Careful, friend, this one is true. Leviticus 19:16 says, “You must not go about spreading slander among your people.” That's a direct command from God, right there in the text. Right next to it comes “You must not endanger the life of your neighbor.” So the passage takes words about a neighbor seriously.

That's it. “Directly rebuke your neighbor…” (Leviticus 19:17) It comes right after “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart.” So instead of keeping it inside, God says to rebuke your neighbor directly. The word is directly, friend.

The priest isn't mentioned in this verse. God says to “Directly rebuke your neighbor…” (Leviticus 19:17) The word is directly, so the neighbor is the one who hears it. That's the instruction as written.

explanations.answer: Let it go and say nothing
explanations.explanation: Saying nothing sounds peaceful, but it's not what the verse says. After “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart.” God adds, “Directly rebuke your neighbor…” (Leviticus 19:17) So the hatred doesn't get to sit in the heart, and the neighbor gets spoken to. God says to speak up.

explanations.answer: So you won't incur guilt over him
explanations.explanation: Right. “Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him.” (Leviticus 19:17) That's the reason God gives, and it's the only one in the verse. It comes right after the command not to harbor hatred in your heart. I think it shows how seriously He takes the way people treat each other.

explanations.answer: So he will owe you an apology
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about an apology being owed. God's reason is, “…so that you will not incur guilt on account of him.” (Leviticus 19:17) So it's about the one speaking, not collecting from the neighbor. That's the reason as written.

explanations.answer: So it never goes before a judge
explanations.explanation: A judge isn't mentioned in this verse. The reason God gives is, “…so that you will not incur guilt on account of him.” (Leviticus 19:17) I know the courtroom is a natural guess, since verse 15 was about judging. But this reason is about guilt.

You got it. “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:18) Notice that it's "but." God doesn't stop at telling them what to drop. He tells them what to pick up instead.

explanations.answer: Keep your distance from your neighbor
explanations.explanation: Distance would be easy, but that's not what God asks. The verse says, “…but love your neighbor as yourself.” (Leviticus 19:18) He swaps revenge and grudges for love. Love goes toward the neighbor.

explanations.answer: Forgive your neighbor once a year
explanations.explanation: There's no yearly schedule in this verse, friend. God says, “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself.” (Leviticus 19:18) It's not a once-a-year thing. Love is the standing command, and it's signed, “I am the LORD…”

That's not what the verse says. God says, “…you shall not wear clothing made of two kinds of material.” (Leviticus 19:19) It sits in the same verse as the livestock and the seed. All three are about not mixing two kinds.

False is right. The verse says, “…you shall not wear clothing made of two kinds of material.” (Leviticus 19:19) It comes right after the two kinds of livestock and the two kinds of seed. The text doesn't say why, so I'll leave it right where God put it.

explanations.answer: It is offered to the LORD in praise
explanations.explanation: That's right. “In the fourth year all its fruit must be consecrated as a praise offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:24) Three years it's forbidden, and then in year four, all of it is offered to Him in praise. All of it, not just some. The eating for Israel comes in the fifth year. (Leviticus 19:25)

explanations.answer: It is stored up for a hard year
explanations.explanation: Storing it up isn't in the verse. God says, “In the fourth year all its fruit must be consecrated as a praise offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:24) So the fourth-year fruit goes to Him. The eating comes after that, in year five.

explanations.answer: It is sold to buy more seed
explanations.explanation: Selling isn't mentioned here. The verse says, “In the fourth year all its fruit must be consecrated as a praise offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:24) The fourth year belongs to praise. It's a year for giving it to Him.

True. “But in the fifth year you may eat its fruit; thus your harvest will be increased.” (Leviticus 19:25) That comes after three forbidden years and a praise offering in year four. Then God signs it, “I am the LORD your God.” So the long wait comes with an increase attached.

It's actually true. The verse says, “But in the fifth year you may eat its fruit; thus your harvest will be increased.” (Leviticus 19:25) Three years forbidden, a year of praise, and then year five you eat. I waited years in the back of a junk drawer, so I won't complain about a few years of waiting on fruit. And God signs it, “I am the LORD your God.”

explanations.answer: They will be defiled by them
explanations.explanation: Yes. “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them.” (Leviticus 19:31) There are two commands in there: don't turn to them, and don't seek them out. The result God names is being defiled by them. And He closes it with “I am the LORD your God.”

The harvest isn't mentioned in this verse. God says not to seek out mediums or spiritists, “…or you will be defiled by them.” (Leviticus 19:31) The result He names is defilement. I'll stick with His word on it.

explanations.answer: They will owe the priest a fine
explanations.explanation: A fine to the priest? Nice try, friend, but no bill shows up in this verse. God says, “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them.” (Leviticus 19:31) The result He names is being defiled by them. I think that's a serious warning, so I'll stay with His words.

That's it. “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God. I am the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:32) When an older person walks in, you stand up. Then you honor them. And God puts fearing Him right in the same verse.

explanations.answer: Wait for them to speak first
explanations.explanation: Speaking order isn't in the verse. God says, “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God.” (Leviticus 19:32) So the actions are to rise and to honor, and the verse adds fearing Him. Waiting for them to speak first isn't there.

Judging disputes isn't part of this verse. God says, “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God.” (Leviticus 19:32) The command is about honor, and it's a short one. Stand up and honor them.

Right. “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born…” (Leviticus 19:34) Not a second-class guest, but one of their own. The verse goes on, “…and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” So God doesn't just say to tolerate him, He says to love him.

explanations.answer: As a guest for one season only
explanations.explanation: The verse puts no time limit on it. God says, “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born…” (Leviticus 19:34) So he's treated as one of their own, not as a visitor on a timer.

explanations.answer: As a hired hand on lower wages
explanations.explanation: Lower wages are the opposite of this command. God says, “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born…” (Leviticus 19:34) And a verse earlier He says, “…you must not oppress him.” (Leviticus 19:33) So he's treated as one of their own.

That's the reason God gives. “…love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.” (Leviticus 19:34) So Israel knows from their own history what it's like to be the outsider. God points them right back to that.

Joining Israel isn't the reason in this verse. God says, “…love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” (Leviticus 19:34) The reason looks backward, to Egypt. It's not about what the foreigner might do later.
Trade doesn't come up here, friend. The reason God gives is, “…for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” (Leviticus 19:34) It's about where Israel has been. God doesn't mention what they'd gain.

Scales, you got it. “You shall maintain honest scales and weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin.” (Leviticus 19:36) An ephah and a hin are both measures, one for dry goods and one for liquid. And God signs it with “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

Coins make sense for money, but the verse doesn't use them. God says, “You shall maintain honest scales and weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin.” (Leviticus 19:36) The words are all about measuring. Honest scales is the match.

No lamps in this verse, friend. It says, “You shall maintain honest scales and weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin.” (Leviticus 19:36) Everything on that list is for measuring. Scales is the one that fits the blank.
